## The idea

A two-minute piece need not contain two minutes of unrelated note data.
Repetition gives the listener something to remember, which in turn makes a
departure legible. When the opening returns after contrasting material, it
carries both its original identity and the time that has passed since it was
last heard.

*Form* is the organisation of sections across the span of a piece. Binary form
uses two large regions; ternary form returns, as in ABA; rondo alternates a
recurring A with contrasting episodes. For construction, a section can resemble
a function and the form plan its call sequence. A varied return invokes familiar
material with altered arguments rather than copying and editing the section.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60
use_synth :prophet

sections = {
  a: [:c4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :f4, :g4, :c5],
  b: [:a3, :c4, :e4, :g4, :f4, :d4, :b3, :g3],
  c: [:f4, :a4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :b3, :c4, :e4],
  transition: [:g3, :a3, :b3, :d4, :f4, :e4, :d4, :g3]
}

define :play_section do |notes, transpose, amp|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play note(pitch) + transpose, sustain: 2.5,
      release: 0.35, amp: amp
    sleep 3
  end
end

form = [
  [:a, 0, 0.65],
  [:b, 0, 0.55],
  [:a, 12, 0.5],
  [:transition, 0, 0.6],
  [:c, 0, 0.7]
]

form.each do |name, transpose, amp|
  puts "section #{name} transpose=#{transpose}"
  play_section sections[name], transpose, amp
end
```

Every section lasts twenty-four beats, so the five calls fill two minutes at 60
BPM. When A returns, it sounds an octave higher and at lower amplitude. The note
data identifies it as the same section, while the arguments let elapsed time
leave a mark on the return. The transition has its own name because connecting
two regions is a distinct formal job, not an anonymous gap.

## Change one thing

1. Call A twice before B. The repetition gives the opening more time to settle
   in memory and postpones contrast. Notice whether the second pass strengthens
   recognition or begins to exhaust the eight-note material.
2. Return A at its original register and amplitude. Compare that literal return
   with the quieter octave version, listening for whether recognition or change
   dominates the moment.
3. Change the plan to A-B-A-C-A. More frequent returns turn the design toward
   rondo and make C an episode framed by familiar material on both sides.

## Why it works

The `sections` hash stores each body of material once. The `form` array records
order and realisation arguments, and `play_section` interprets both. Large-scale
revision can therefore happen in a short, visible plan without duplicating note
lists. When A changes at the source, all of its returns remain related.

A section name claims identity; its arguments describe variation. Transposition
preserves interval relationships while changing register, and amplitude changes
the listener's perspective on the material. Other arguments might select
instrumentation, articulation, or omitted phrases. If variation erases the
recognisable features of a section, assigning a new name may describe the heard
result more accurately than insisting it remains A.

The control-flow analogy has a boundary. A listener hears a return through
memory of everything that intervened, while a runtime assigns no emotional
weight to the second call of a function. The analogy remains useful for making
the piece: define reusable units, order them, parameterise legitimate changes,
and keep that form plan separate from the details of rendering.

Code boundaries also need audible evidence. A new key, register, texture,
cadence, or rhythmic profile can announce B. Changing a symbol in the array does
nothing by itself if B behaves like A. The printed labels support inspection,
but a listener who cannot see the log should still hear the same divisions.

A transition deserves explicit data when it changes the route between sections.
Here it lasts as long as A, B, or C, which may cause it to sound like a fourth
section rather than a bridge. Shorten it to four notes and compare its apparent
function. Formal labels are analytical judgements supported by proportion and
behaviour; the renderer does not enforce them as types.

Distance in time changes repetition too. A return after twenty seconds may feel
like immediate confirmation; after a minute, the same notes can feel recovered
from memory. Keeping the order in a visible array makes those spans measurable
and easy to revise. The call is unchanged, but its position gives it a new
formal consequence.

## Take it further

Compose an A-B-A-C-A rondo of at least ninety seconds. Store A once and render
its returns with two different argument sets. Give B and C distinct pitch ranges
and rhythmic profiles so the contrast survives without printed labels. Keep the
form as data, include one named transition, and copy no section arrays. Print
each section name during playback, then listen once without the log and mark the
boundaries you can actually hear.
